item.title: MiBeeNvr: From v0.1.0 to v0.12.0
item.description: MiBeeNvr is an NVR built for a home camera fleet. v0.1.0 shipped on May 6, 2026; v0.12.0 on September 1 — twelve releases in a bit over four months. This post merges the per-release notes from v0.1.0 through v0.12.0 into one timeline: what each step did, and why. The house style for mechanisms is plain words first, then a picture, then the parameters. The v0.13.0 performance benchmarks are a separate post, linked at the end.

item.title: ONVIF vs GB/T 28181: How They Work Inside — Plug-and-Play Devices vs System-Level Networking
item.description: After MiBeeNvr v0.9 shipped ONVIF auto-discovery, manual camera configuration was mostly gone. The next question was whether to add GB/T 28181 uplink support, so I dug through the mechanics of both protocols. Most comparison articles online stop at “ONVIF is the international standard, GB28181 is the Chinese national standard”—which carries zero information for someone writing code. This post breaks both protocols down to the signaling-flow and message level: how ONVIF discovers devices and obtains stream URIs; how GB28181’s 20-digit codes address everything, how INVITE negotiates a stream, and what PS encapsulation actually is.

item.title: The Surveillance Protocol Panorama: A Four-Layer Map from Access to Compliance — What Each Protocol Is and When to Use It
item.description: The previous post took ONVIF and GB/T 28181 apart down to signaling and messages. But building an NVR means the protocol environment extends well beyond those two: vendor-private APIs on the camera side, a view-library standard on the public-security side, Ministry-of-Transport standards for vehicles, WebRTC for browser viewing, HLS for public distribution, and a national-crypto compliance stack. This post lays out the entire landscape—each protocol gets four sections: what it is → key technical points → its relationship with other protocols → its value to an NVR. Beginners can read it as an index; veterans can jump straight to the priority table.

item.title: Dual-Stack Cameras in the Field: What Happens When ONVIF and GB28181 Run Together, and Whether GB28181 Travels
item.description:
The first two posts covered protocol mechanics and the landscape; this one returns to device-side questions an NVR builder actually meets: can a camera hang both protocol stacks at once? With both enabled, what does it cost the camera, and what does it mean for an NVR that discovers cameras via ONVIF? Finally, a product question—does GB28181 actually get used overseas, and is it worth building for international markets?

item.title: The Rust and Go Ecosystems for ONVIF/GB28181: Library Selection, Source Reading, and a Hardware-Free Integration Path
item.description: The first three posts settled the protocol mechanics, the landscape, and the device side; the final question is concrete: which libraries to write it with. This survey went through everything usable in both ecosystems. The one-sentence verdict: ONVIF has workable libraries on both sides; the mature GB28181 implementations live on the Go/Java/C++ side while Rust’s are still young; and for streaming infrastructure (repackaging, distribution, egress) the Go ecosystem is clearly thicker.

item.title: Four Protocol Libraries, Extracted: ONVIF and GB28181 in Go and Rust
item.description:
MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols. ONVIF is the de facto standard internationally — Hikvision, Axis, Dahua, and Bosch all speak it. GB/T 28181 is China’s national surveillance standard, unavoidable in government and state-owned projects. The device side (Raspberry Pi camera firmware, one Go and one Rust implementation) and the NVR side (MiBeeNvr, Go) both speak these two protocols, and the stacks have always lived inside the projects.

Two problems with that. First, this code is pickled in interop details — digest-auth qop handling, SIP Via-branch uniqueness, MANSCDP element-vs-attribute dual forms, TCP framing header byte counts — each one was ground out against a real platform, and a new project would have to grind them all again. Second, a library survey two weeks ago showed the open-source landscape for these protocols is unevenly populated; several positions have no one standing in them.

item.title: The Protocol Library Family Grows to Five: onvif-go Reaches v2 and the GB28181 Device Side Wraps Up
item.description: MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols: ONVIF, the de facto standard internationally that Hikvision, Axis, and Dahua all speak, and GB/T 28181, China’s national surveillance standard that government and state-owned projects cannot avoid. The protocol stack is open-sourced as five independent libraries split by protocol × language × role, all extracted from production code, and in the latest release round all five tagged on the same day: onvif-go entered the stable v2 line, onvif-device-rs shipped to crates.io, gb28181-go and gb28181-rs closed out the 2022 device-side surface, and onvif-c debuted as the fifth member. This post goes library by library through capability boundaries, key design decisions, and remaining limitations, stated as released.

item.title: gb28181-go Tutorial: From Device Registration to Platform Ingest
item.description: gb28181-go is the only all-in-one volume among the five protocol libraries: the same module carries the device side (UAC, registering a media source to a GB/T 28181 platform) and the platform side (UAS, accepting device registrations and pulling streams from them). The device code came out of the MiBee Eye Raspberry Pi camera firmware, and the platform side was extracted wholesale from MiBeeNvr’s GB28181 access implementation — the two ends bite against each other in production every day.

item.title: gb28181-rs Tutorial: Registering a Device to a GB28181 Platform in Rust
item.description: gb28181-rs is the Rust implementation of the GB/T 28181 device side (UAC): register a media source to a national-standard platform, push streams to it, and receive platform-pushed controls. It is a twin of gb28181-go — the same responsibilities in two languages, with PTZ bit decoding, talk-back SDP, and snapshots sharing one set of golden wire-format tables, so whichever packaging drifts turns red first. The library was extracted from MiBee’s Rust camera firmware and runs in production daily.
